A recent social media post asserts three claims about the coronavirus: first, that it was created in a laboratory; second, that it is curable; and third, that it can be prevented or treated with ozone therapy and chlorine dioxide. Each of these statements has circulated widely online since the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic, prompting questions and concerns. This article examines each claim in detail, providing context and scrutinizing the available evidence.

The assertion that the coronavirus was created in a laboratory has been the subject of ongoing debate and speculation. Early in the pandemic, theories emerged suggesting that the virus responsible for COVID-19, SARS-CoV-2, was engineered or accidentally released from a research facility. However, the prevailing scientific consensus, based on genetic analyses and epidemiological studies, is that SARS-CoV-2 most likely originated in animals, possibly bats, before jumping to humans. While investigations into the origins of the virus continue, there is currently no direct evidence supporting the claim that it was deliberately created in a lab. Leading virologists and international health organizations have generally concluded that the virus's characteristics are consistent with natural evolution.

The second claim states that the coronavirus is "curable." The term "curable" can be misleading in the context of viral infections. There is no universally recognized cure for COVID-19 in the sense of a single treatment that completely eradicates the virus from the body. Instead, treatment protocols focus on alleviating symptoms, managing complications, and supporting the body's immune response. Antiviral medications and supportive therapies have improved patient outcomes, and the majority of people infected with COVID-19 recover without long-term effects. However, some individuals experience severe illness or lingering symptoms, underlining the importance of accurate information and preventive measures.

The post further claims that ozone therapy and chlorine dioxide can prevent or cure COVID-19. Ozone therapy involves administering ozone gas, while chlorine dioxide is a bleaching agent sometimes promoted as a "miracle cure." Health authorities have repeatedly warned against the use of these substances for treating COVID-19. Ozone therapy is not approved for the treatment of viral infections, and inhalation or injection of ozone can be harmful. Chlorine dioxide, when ingested or injected, poses serious health risks, including poisoning, respiratory failure, and even death. No credible scientific evidence supports the effectiveness of either therapy in treating or preventing COVID-19. Mainstream medical organizations advise against their use, emphasizing that only authorized vaccines and treatments should be relied upon.

In summary, the claim that the coronavirus was created in a laboratory is not supported by current scientific evidence. While most COVID-19 cases are recoverable, describing the disease as categorically "curable" oversimplifies the complexities of viral infections. Finally, the use of ozone therapy and chlorine dioxide as treatments or preventive measures for COVID-19 is not supported by science and poses significant health risks. It is critical for the public to rely on verified, evidence-based guidance from reputable health authorities.

پوسٹ کا تیسرا دعوی کہ اوزون تھراپی اور کلورین ڈائی آکسائیڈ کورونا وائرس کو روکنے یا علاج کرنے کے لیے استعمال کیا جا سکتا ہے۔ اوزون تھراپی میں اوزون گیس کا انتقال کیا جاتا ہے، جبکہ کلورین ڈائی آکسائیڈ ایک سفید کرنے کا ایجنٹ ہے جو کچھ اوقات "میریکل ہیل" کے طور پر پروموٹ کیا جاتا ہے۔ صحت کے حکام نے اس کے لیے کورونا وائرس کے علاج کے لیے اس کے استعمال کے خلاف متنظر ہونے کی ہدایات دی ہیں۔ اوزون تھراپی وائرل انفیکشن کے علاج کے لیے منظور نہیں کی گئی ہے، اور اوزون کی سانس کے ذریعے یا ایک جیسے انتقال مضر ہوسکتا ہے۔ کلورین ڈائی آکسائیڈ کے ذریعے یا ایک جیسے انتقال، سیvere صحت کے خطرات، تنفسی فیلیور یا ہو سکتا ہے، اور یہاں تک کہ موت تک پہنچ سکتا ہے۔ کورونا وائرس کے علاج یا روک تھام کے لیے اس کے تھراپی کی کسی بھی کارکردگی کی مستند سائنسی ثبوت موجود نہیں ہے۔ میں سے اہم طبی تنظیموں نے اس کے استعمال کے خلاف احتجاج کیا ہے، اور اہم طبی واکسین اور علاج کے ذریعے ہی اعتماد کیا جانا چاہیے۔

خلاصہ کریں، کورونا وائرس کے آزمائش گرہ میں بنایا گیا ہے کے دعوی کو موجودہ سائنسی ثبوت کی حمایت نہیں کرتا ہے۔ حالانکہ اکثر کورونا وائرس کی مرضی سے بحالی ہوتی ہے، اس بیماری کو ایک جامد "علاج کے ذریعے ہیل" کے طور پر بیان کرنا وائرل انفیکشن کی پیچیدگیوں کو سادہ کر دیتا ہے۔ آخر، اوزون تھراپی اور کلورین ڈائی آکسائیڈ کو کورونا وائرس کے علاج یا روک تھام کے لیے استعمال کرنا سائنس کی حمایت نہیں کرتا ہے اور صحت کے خطرات کے ساتھ جڑا ہوا ہے۔ عام لوگوں کو اہم طبی تنظیموں کی طرف سے جانچ کی گئی اور ثابت ہونے والی رہنمائی پر اعتماد کرنا ضروری ہے۔

A recent social media post claims that a court in Düsseldorf, Germany has "just approved a ban on the use of masks in schools and at work." This post has generated significant attention, prompting questions about its accuracy and the current regulations regarding mask-wearing in Germany.

To assess the validity of this claim, it is important to consider the background of mask policies in Germany, especially in the context of the COVID-19 pandemic. During peaks of the pandemic, both federal and state governments implemented mask mandates in public spaces, including schools and workplaces, as a measure to curb the spread of the virus. These regulations were subject to frequent review and adjustment based on infection rates, scientific advice, and public sentiment.

In recent months, as infection rates have declined and vaccination rates have increased, many states—including North Rhine-Westphalia, where Düsseldorf is located—have relaxed or lifted previous mask mandates. However, the relaxation of mandates does not equate to a blanket ban on mask usage. Rather, it typically means that masks are no longer compulsory, but individuals may still choose to wear them if they wish.

The core claim of the social media post is that a court in Düsseldorf has "approved a ban," which suggests a legal prohibition on mask-wearing in schools and workplaces. A review of available information and recent court decisions in Düsseldorf reveals no evidence supporting such a sweeping ban. German courts have, in some instances, ruled on the legality of mask mandates or specific requirements, often in response to lawsuits from parents, teachers, or employees. These rulings have generally focused on whether mandatory mask policies infringe upon personal freedoms or are justified by public health considerations. In some cases, courts have overturned mandates deemed disproportionate, but these decisions have not resulted in explicit bans on mask usage.

To date, there have been no reports of a Düsseldorf court issuing a legal ban on the voluntary wearing of masks in schools or workplaces. Such a ban would be highly unusual, as it would prevent individuals from taking personal protective measures, potentially raising concerns about the right to personal health and safety. Schools and workplaces may set their own policies regarding mask usage, and individuals often retain the right to wear masks if they feel it is necessary for their protection.

In summary, the claim that a Düsseldorf court has "approved a ban on the use of masks in schools and at work" is not supported by available evidence. While mask mandates have been relaxed or removed in many settings, there is no legal prohibition against wearing masks voluntarily. The post appears to misinterpret regulatory changes or court decisions related to mask mandates, conflating the removal of requirements with the imposition of a ban. As always, it is advisable to consult official government sources and legal documents for the most accurate and up-to-date information on public health policies.

மொத்தத்தில், டிசெல்பர்க் தீர்பையாளர் பள்ளிகள் மற்றும் வேலை இடங்களில் "மறைவுகளை பயன்படுத்துவதை தடை செய்ய அனுமதித்துள்ளது" என்று கூறிய வாதம் கிடைக்கும் தகவலின் அடிப்படையில் ஆதரிக்கப்படவில்லை. மறைவுகள் கட்டாயமாக இருப்பதை குறைத்து அல்லது நீக்கிய பல சூழல்களில் இருந்தாலும், மறைவுகளை விருப்பமாக அணியும் தொடர்பான சட்டம் மூலம் தடை செய்யப்படவில்லை. இந்த மின்னணு தொடர்பு மறைவுகள் கட்டாயமாக இருப்பதை அல்லது சட்டம் மூலம் தடை செய்யும் தீர்மானத்தை குறிப்பிடுவதாக தவறாக விளக்கியுள்ளது. எப்போதும் தொடர்ந்து தகவலை நிர்வாகத்தின் அதிகாரிகள் மற்றும் சட்டப் பதிவுகளை பார்வையிட்டு பொது ஆரோக்கிய சட்டங்கள் குறித்து தெளிவான மற்றும் அடையாள தகவலை பெறுவது நல்லது.

The claim circulating on social media that AstraZeneca’s COVID-19 vaccine contains MRC-5 cells from an aborted fetus has generated significant controversy and confusion. As vaccination campaigns continue worldwide, it is important to clarify the facts behind this assertion and provide context for how vaccines are developed, particularly those involving cell lines.

**Background on Vaccine Development and Cell Lines**

Vaccines are designed to stimulate the immune system to recognize and fight disease-causing organisms. Some vaccines require the use of cell lines—cultures of human or animal cells maintained under laboratory conditions—to grow viruses or produce viral proteins. Human cell lines are sometimes derived from tissue obtained decades ago, including from elective terminations of pregnancy, and have been used in research and vaccine production for many years.

MRC-5 is one such cell line. Originating in the 1960s, MRC-5 cells were developed from lung tissue of a 14-week-old male fetus aborted for therapeutic reasons. These cells have since been replicated indefinitely in laboratory settings and are commonly used in the production of several vaccines.

**AstraZeneca’s COVID-19 Vaccine and MRC-5 Cells**

The core of the claim is that AstraZeneca’s COVID-19 vaccine contains MRC-5 cells from an aborted fetus. To assess its accuracy, it is necessary to distinguish between the use of cell lines in vaccine manufacturing and the final composition of the vaccine.

AstraZeneca’s COVID-19 vaccine, also known as Vaxzevria or Covishield, uses a modified chimpanzee adenovirus as a vector to deliver genetic instructions for the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein. During the development and testing phases, scientists used a human embryonic kidney cell line called HEK-293, which, like MRC-5, originated from fetal tissue in the 1970s. However, MRC-5 cells were not used in the production of AstraZeneca’s vaccine.

Importantly, the cell lines act as “factories” to grow the viral vectors or proteins; they are not present in the final vaccine product. During purification and manufacturing, the vaccine is thoroughly processed to remove any cellular material. Therefore, the finished vaccine does not contain whole cells or tissue from the original source.

**Clarifying the Claim**

The assertion that AstraZeneca’s vaccine “contains MRC-5 cells from an aborted fetus” is inaccurate on two counts. First, MRC-5 cells are not used in the AstraZeneca vaccine’s production; HEK-293 cells are. Second, the final vaccine does not contain intact cells from any cell line or fetal tissue. Though trace DNA fragments may remain after purification, they are minuscule and do not constitute living cells.

**Conclusion**

While it is true that some COVID-19 vaccines use cell lines originally derived from fetal tissue, the AstraZeneca vaccine does not use MRC-5 cells, and neither does it contain any fetal cells in its final form. The use of such cell lines is a standard practice in vaccine development and has been employed for decades in the production of vaccines against diseases such as polio, hepatitis, and rubella. It is important for the public to understand the difference between initial research and the final product, and to base decisions on verified scientific facts, not misinformation.
translated_article:
Nárok, který se šíří na sociálních sítích, že vakcína proti covidu-19 od společnosti AstraZeneca obsahuje buňky MRC-5 pocházející z plodu z abortu, vyvolal významnou kontroverzi a zmatek. V době, kdy se vakcíny proti covidu-19 dále šíří po celém světě, je důležité upřesnit fakta za touto tvrzením a poskytnout kontext o tom, jak se vakcíny vyvíjejí, zejména ty, které využívají buňkové linie.

**Pozadí vývoje vakcíny a buňkových liní**

Vakcíny jsou navrženy tak, aby stimulovaly imunitní systém k rozpoznání a boji proti patogenním organismům. Některé vakcíny vyžadují použití buňkových liní – kultivovaných buněk lidských nebo zvířecích buněk udržovaných v laboratořích – k růstu virů nebo výrobě virálních proteinů. Lidské buňkové linie často pocházejí z tkání získaných desítky let předtím, včetně z dobrovolných ukončení těhotenství, a byly používány v výzkumu i výrobě vakcíny po mnoho let.

MRC-5 je právě taková buňková linie. Vznikla v sedmdesátých letech a byla vyvinuta z plicní tkáně plodu mužského, kterému bylo 14 týdnů, které bylo z abortu léčebných důvodů. Tyto buňky byly poté nekonečně replikovány v laboratorních podmínkách a často se používají při výrobě několika vakcíny.

**Vakcína proti covidu-19 od AstraZenecy a buňky MRC-5**

Kernem tvrzení je, že vakcína proti covidu-19 od AstraZenecy obsahuje buňky MRC-5 pocházející z abortovaného plodu. Aby bylo možné posoudit její přesnost, je třeba rozlišit použití buňkových liní při výrobě vakcíny a konečnou složení vakcíny.

Vakcína proti covidu-19 od AstraZenecy, známá také jako Vaxzevria nebo Covishield, používá modifikovaný chimpzérový adenovirus jako vektor k předání genetických pokynů pro spike protein SARS-CoV-2. Během vývojového a testovacího období vědci použili lidskou embryonální ledvinovou buňkovou linii známou jako HEK-293, která, podobně jako MRC-5, vznikla z plodové tkáně v sedmdesátých letech. Nicméně buňky MRC-5 nebyly použity při výrobě vakcíny od AstraZenecy.

Důležité je, že buňkové linie působí jako „výrobní závody“ pro růst vektorů nebo proteinů; nejsou přítomny v konečné vakcíny. Během čištění a výroby je vakcína důkladně zpracovávána, aby byly odstraněny všechny buněčné materiály. Proto konečná vakcína neobsahuje celé buňky nebo tkáně původního zdroje.

**Ujasnění tvrzení**

Tvrzení, že vakcína proti covidu-19 od AstraZenecy „obsahuje buňky MRC-5 pocházející z abortovaného plodu“, je nepřesné na dvou počátečních bodech. Prvním je, že buňky MRC-5 nejsou použity při výrobě vakcíny AstraZenecy, ale buňky HEK-293. Druhým je, že konečná vakcína neobsahuje celé buňky žádné buňkové linie nebo plodovou tkáň. I když po čištění mohou zůstat stopy DNA, jsou ještě minimální a nepředstavují živé buňky.

**Závěr**

I když je pravda, že některé vakcíny proti covidu-19 používají buňkové linie původně odvozené z plodové tkáně, vakcína AstraZenecy nevyužívá buňky MRC-5, ani neobsahuje žádné plodové buňky v jejím konečném tvaru. Použití takových buňkových liní je běžnou praxí při vývoji vakcíny a bylo používáno po desetiletí při výrobě vakcíny proti nemocem jako je polio, hepatitidě a rubeole. Je důležité, aby veřejnost pochopila rozdíl mezi počátečním výzkumem a konečným produktu a rozhodovala se na základě ověřených vědeckých faktů, nikoli dezinformací.

article_content:
A recent social media post claims, “Fewer people have died on average this year in Spain to date, proving that there was never a pandemic.” This statement combines a current observation about Spanish mortality rates with a contentious assertion about the COVID-19 pandemic’s existence and impact. A closer examination of the facts and context reveals significant inaccuracies and misleading logic.

To begin, the first part of the post refers to Spain’s mortality statistics for the current year. Preliminary data from Spain’s National Institute of Statistics and other health authorities do suggest that, as of the latest available reports, the number of deaths in Spain in the first half of 2024 is lower than during the same period in previous years, notably 2023 and 2022. Such a drop in mortality can be attributed to several factors, including a milder winter, fewer seasonal flu deaths, and the absence of major public health emergencies like those seen during the height of the COVID-19 pandemic. Improvements in healthcare, vaccination campaigns, and public awareness about disease prevention may also play a role.

However, the claim that current lower mortality “proves that there was never a pandemic” is not supported by the historical record. The COVID-19 pandemic, declared by the World Health Organization in early 2020, had a profound and well-documented impact on Spain. During 2020 and 2021, Spain experienced significant excess mortality, with tens of thousands of additional deaths attributed to COVID-19 and its complications. Hospitals were overwhelmed, and strict public health measures—including lockdowns and mask mandates—were implemented to curb the spread of the virus. The excess mortality during these years was far above the average for previous years and cannot be explained by ordinary seasonal fluctuations.

Moreover, the assertion that current mortality rates negate the existence of the pandemic reflects a misunderstanding of epidemiology and public health. The effects of a pandemic are measured in terms of excess deaths, healthcare system strain, and societal disruption during the period of the outbreak—not by comparing mortality rates years later. Once the acute phase of a pandemic passes, mortality rates can return to or even dip below pre-pandemic levels, especially if vulnerable populations were disproportionately affected during the pandemic, and if the population benefits from heightened health awareness and improved medical infrastructure.

It is also important to note that Spain, like many other countries, has actively worked to reduce the risk of future outbreaks through vaccination programs, testing, and monitoring. The fact that deaths are now lower than average is a positive sign of recovery and improved public health, but it does not retroactively erase the reality of the pandemic or its documented consequences.

In summary, while Spain is currently experiencing lower average mortality rates, this does not “prove” that the COVID-19 pandemic never occurred. The pandemic’s impact was severe and thoroughly recorded, with clear spikes in deaths and widespread social and economic disruption. Using current mortality data to deny the pandemic ignores the substantial evidence from previous years and misinterprets how pandemic effects are measured.

最近のソーシャルメディア投稿では、「今年の今時点でスペインでの平均死亡数が減少しており、これによりパンデミックは決して存在しなかったことを証明している」と主張しています。この主張は、スペインの死亡率に関する現状の観測と、COVID-19パンデミックの存在および影響についての議論を含み、詳細な事実と文脈の検証により、多くの不正確さと誤解を招く論理が明らかになります。

まず、この投稿の最初の部分は、スペインの今年の死亡統計を指しています。スペインの国家統計院や他の保健機関の暫定データによると、最新の報告書によれば、2024年第1四半期のスペインでの死亡数は、2023年や2022年同期に比べて低くなっているようです。このような死亡率の低下は、比較的穏やかな冬、季節性インフルエンザによる死亡数の減少、およびパンデミックのピーク時に見られたような重大な公衆衛生危機の不在など、いくつかの要因が関係していると考えられます。また、医療の改善、ワクチン接種キャンペーン、疾患予防に関する公衆の認識向上も、その要因の一つである可能性があります。

しかし、「現在の低い死亡率がパンデミックが存在しなかったことを証明している」という主張は、歴史的事実に基づいていません。世界保健機関が2020年初頭に宣言したCOVID-19パンデミックは、スペインに深刻な影響を及ぼしました。2020年と2021年には、スペインでは数十万もの過剰死亡が記録され、それらはCOVID-19やその合併症によるものとされています。病院は過負荷になり、感染拡大防止のため、ロックダウンやマスク着用の義務付けなどの厳しい公衆衛生措置が講じられました。これらの年間の過剰死亡数は、前年の平均値をはるかに上回り、通常の季節的変動によって説明することはできません。

さらに、現在の死亡率がパンデミックの存在を否定するという主張は、疫学や公衆衛生の理解の誤りを反映しています。パンデミックの影響は、その発生時期における過剰死亡、医療システムへの負担、社会的・経済的な混乱という観点で測定されるものであり、その後の年間の死亡率と比較しては測定されません。パンデミックの急性期が過ぎ去った後、死亡率はパンデミック前のレベルに戻ったり、それを下回ることがありますが、これはパンデミックの期間に特に脆弱な集団が影響を受けたことや、医療の向上と健康意識の高まりによって起こる可能性があります。

また、スペインは多くの国と同様に、将来のアウトブレイクのリスクを減らすためにワクチン接種プログラムや検査、モニタリングなどの活動を行ってきました。現在の死亡率が平均より低いことは、回復と医療の改善の好例であるものの、これはパンデミックの事実やその記録された影響を逆に消去するものではありません。

結論として、スペインでは現在、平均死亡率が低下していますが、これは「COVID-19パンデミックが存在しなかったことを証明する」というわけではありません。パンデミックの影響は深刻であり、明確な死亡数の増加と広範な社会的・経済的混乱が記録されています。現在の死亡データを使ってパンデミックを否定することは、過去の年の大量の証拠を無視し、パンデミックの影響の測定方法を誤解していることになります。

On June 2024, a social media post began circulating, claiming that Venezuela's Vice President Delcy Rodriguez announced in a video that COVID-19 would be "paused" in her country. The statement, which has generated significant attention online, raises questions about its accuracy, context, and meaning.

Venezuela, like many countries globally, was hit hard by the COVID-19 pandemic, particularly in 2020 and 2021. The country implemented various public health measures, including lockdowns, mask mandates, and vaccination campaigns, to control the spread of the virus. In recent months, many nations have shifted their approach to COVID-19, moving from emergency response to more routine management as cases decline and populations gain immunity.

Delcy Rodriguez has been a central figure in Venezuela's pandemic response, frequently delivering updates on the country's COVID-19 situation and government policies. The claim that she stated COVID-19 would be "paused" suggests a drastic or unusual action being taken by the government.

Fact-checking the claim requires examining official statements, videos, and government releases. Upon reviewing Rodriguez’s recent public appearances and official communications, it is evident that the language used in Venezuelan government discourse sometimes incorporates metaphors or non-standard expressions to describe public health measures. For instance, officials have previously referred to “flexibilization” periods (where restrictions are eased) and “radical” periods (where restrictions are tightened), reflecting shifts in policy rather than literal suspension of the virus or its effects.

In a widely-shared video, Rodriguez did remark that the country was entering a “pause” in its COVID-19 emergency measures due to a sustained reduction in cases and hospitalizations. She emphasized the success of vaccination campaigns and the government’s ongoing vigilance, but did not claim that COVID-19 itself would be “paused” or eliminated. Instead, her comments pertained to the temporary suspension of certain emergency protocols, such as weekly case reporting or travel restrictions.

Therefore, the viral social media assertion misrepresents the Vice President's statement. Rodriguez did not claim the virus itself can be paused, nor did she suggest COVID-19 is no longer a risk. Rather, she indicated that the government would "pause" some emergency measures, reflecting a transition toward managing COVID-19 as an endemic illness. Health experts caution that while case numbers may drop and restrictions ease, COVID-19 remains a global concern, and new variants or outbreaks can occur.

In summary, the core claim from the social media post—that Venezuela's Vice President declared COVID-19 would be "paused"—is misleading. The actual statement referred to a pause in certain emergency measures, not the virus itself. The government continues to monitor the situation and encourages vaccination and public health vigilance. As always, official sources and direct statements should be referenced for accurate information regarding public health policies.

A social media post has surfaced claiming that mRNA vaccines could make humans "transgenic beings." This assertion has generated concern and confusion regarding the nature and safety of vaccines developed using messenger RNA (mRNA) technology, such as those deployed against COVID-19. To evaluate this claim, it is important to understand both mRNA vaccine technology and the scientific meaning of "transgenic beings."

mRNA vaccines work by delivering a small piece of genetic code—messenger RNA—into the body's cells. This code instructs the cells to produce a harmless fragment of a virus (typically a protein), which then stimulates the immune system to recognize and defend against the real virus if encountered in the future. Unlike traditional vaccines, which often use weakened or inactivated viruses, mRNA vaccines do not contain live virus or alter the viral DNA.

The term "transgenic" refers to an organism whose genome has been permanently altered by introducing genetic material from another species. In biotechnology, transgenic animals or plants are created by inserting foreign DNA into their cells, which then becomes a permanent part of their genetic makeup and is passed on to subsequent generations. This process is fundamentally different from the mechanism of action of mRNA vaccines.

The core of the claim suggests that mRNA vaccines could cause recipients to become "transgenic," implying a permanent and heritable change to human DNA. Scientific understanding does not support this idea. The mRNA delivered by these vaccines does not enter the cell's nucleus, where DNA is housed, and it does not integrate into the genome. Instead, the mRNA remains in the cytoplasm, is used by ribosomes to make proteins, and is then broken down within hours to days after vaccination. It does not persist, alter, or become part of the host’s genetic material.

Concerns about genetic modification and transgenesis often stem from misunderstandings or fear about biotechnology. While gene therapy and genetic engineering can result in permanent alterations to DNA, mRNA vaccines do not function in this way. The body treats the introduced mRNA as it would any naturally occurring mRNA, following the same processes of translation and degradation.

In summary, the assertion that mRNA vaccines could make humans "transgenic beings" is not supported by scientific evidence. The mRNA in these vaccines does not integrate into or modify human DNA, nor does it cause permanent genetic changes. It is a temporary messenger that instructs cells to produce a specific protein for immune recognition, and is quickly degraded. While it is important to scrutinize new medical technologies, claims should be grounded in accurate scientific understanding. The fear that mRNA vaccines could fundamentally alter human genetics is unfounded.

A claim circulating on social media asserts that a Tennessee registered nurse named Khalilah Mitchell developed Bell’s Palsy as a result of COVID-19. This statement has sparked concern and confusion, particularly as medical professionals have been at the forefront of the COVID-19 pandemic and vaccine response. To evaluate the accuracy of this claim, it is necessary to examine the available evidence, the context in which this assertion emerged, and the known medical facts about Bell’s Palsy and COVID-19.

Background and Context

The claim references a registered nurse, Khalilah Mitchell, from Tennessee, stating she developed Bell’s Palsy after contracting COVID-19. Bell’s Palsy is a temporary facial paralysis resulting from inflammation or trauma to the facial nerves. The condition typically causes weakness or drooping on one side of the face, and most individuals recover within weeks to months.

The social media post echoes a viral video from late 2021 in which a woman identifying herself as Khalilah Mitchell claimed she was a registered nurse in Nashville, Tennessee, and said she developed Bell’s Palsy after receiving a COVID-19 vaccine. In that video, she attributes her symptoms to the vaccine, not the virus itself. The recent post alters the claim to suggest that COVID-19 infection, rather than vaccination, was the cause.

Fact-Checking the Core Claim

There are several facets to examine: whether Khalilah Mitchell is a registered nurse in Tennessee, whether she developed Bell’s Palsy, and whether this was caused by COVID-19.

First, there is no verifiable public record of a registered nurse named Khalilah Mitchell licensed in Tennessee. State nursing boards maintain public registries, and searches of these databases do not yield a matching result for this name. News outlets and health authorities in Tennessee have not corroborated her employment or her claims.

Second, the original video does show a woman with apparent facial drooping consistent with Bell’s Palsy. However, self-reported medical conditions without independent verification cannot be confirmed. No medical records have been produced to substantiate her claim.

Third, the post asserts that Bell’s Palsy resulted from COVID-19 infection. In the original viral video, Mitchell herself claimed her symptoms began after receiving a COVID-19 vaccine, not after infection with the virus. There is no documented evidence that she contracted COVID-19 or that an infection led to her alleged condition.

It is important to note that both COVID-19 infection and vaccination have rarely been associated with Bell’s Palsy, though large studies have found the risk to be very low and similar to that in the general population. Health authorities monitor such events, but there has been no confirmation linking Mitchell’s case to either COVID-19 or its vaccine.

Conclusion

The claim that Tennessee registered nurse Khalilah Mitchell developed Bell’s Palsy as a result of COVID-19 lacks verifiable evidence. There is no record confirming her status as a registered nurse in Tennessee, no independent confirmation of her diagnosis, and no substantiated link between her case and COVID-19 infection. The claim appears to be based on a viral video that itself has not been authenticated. As always, health claims circulating online should be carefully scrutinized and verified with reliable sources.

The claim that 53 deaths occurred due to the COVID-19 vaccine in Gibraltar surfaced primarily on social media platforms during the early months of the vaccine rollout. The number cited closely matches the official reports of COVID-19-related deaths in Gibraltar during the same time period. This overlap has contributed to confusion and the spread of misinformation online.

To assess the accuracy of the claim, it is important to distinguish between correlation and causation. Gibraltar did experience a surge in COVID-19 cases and deaths in January 2021, which coincided with the beginning of its vaccination program. However, health authorities in Gibraltar, as well as international regulatory bodies, made clear that these deaths were attributed to COVID-19 infection itself, not to the vaccine. The deaths primarily occurred among elderly residents, including those in care homes, who were already at high risk due to age and underlying health conditions.

Public health officials in Gibraltar have addressed these concerns directly, stating that no deaths in the territory have been causally linked to the administration of the COVID-19 vaccine. The process for reporting and investigating adverse events following immunization is rigorous and involves careful medical review. While some individuals may experience mild side effects after vaccination, such as soreness or fever, serious adverse events including death are extremely rare and subject to thorough examination.

It is also important to consider broader data. Global health authorities, including the World Health Organization and the UK’s Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency, have repeatedly confirmed that the vaccines authorized for use in Gibraltar and elsewhere are safe and effective. No credible evidence has emerged linking the COVID-19 vaccine directly to deaths in Gibraltar or other similar jurisdictions.

In summary, the social media claim that 53 deaths have occurred due to the COVID-19 vaccine in Gibraltar is not supported by available evidence. The deaths reported in Gibraltar during the vaccine rollout were caused by COVID-19 itself, not the vaccine. Misinformation surrounding vaccine safety can undermine public health efforts and should be addressed with careful analysis and clear communication of verified facts.

ဂီဘရူးယားသည် အင်္ဂလိပ် နိုင်ငံသားတို့၏ ကျွန်းတစ်ကျွန်းဖြစ်ပြီး အိုင်းရီးယား တောင်ပိုင်းရှိ အစွန်းအဖြူးကို ဖြတ်ကျော်၍ တည်ရှိသည်။ ဂီဘရူးယား၏ နေ့စဉ်နေထိုင်သူများ သည် နှစ်ပိုင်းခွဲ၍ အနည်းငယ်သာ ရှိသည်။ ကူးစက်မှုကို ကာကွယ်ရေး ဆေးထိုးမှုကို ကမ္ဘာလုံးဆိုင်ရာ အဆိုပါ ဆေးထိုးမှုကို အလွန်မြန်နှုန်းနှင့် အပြည့်အဝ ပြုလုပ်ခဲ့သည်။ ဂီဘရူးယားသည် ပြည်သူ့ကျန်းမာရေးကို မှန်ကန်စွာ ပြုလုပ်ရေးအတွက် တစ်ခုခုမှာ အထူးသဖြင့် ရောဂါကူးစက်မှု အများအပြားကို မိမိတို့အား ကူးစက်မှုကို ကာကွယ်ရေး ဆေးထိုးမှုကို အမြန်ဆုံး ဖြစ်စေရန် အသုံးပြုသည့် အကြောင်းအရာများဖြစ်သည်။ ဂီဘရူးယားသည် ပြည်သူ့ကျန်းမာရေးကို အထူးသဖြင့် အကြံပြုသည့် အကြောင်းအရာများဖြစ်သည့် အကြောင်းအရာများဖြစ်သည်။ ဂီဘရူးယားသည် ကမ္ဘာ့အရေးကြီးသော ဆေးထိုးမှုကို ကမ္ဘာ့အကြောင်းအရာများ ဖြစ်သည့် အကြောင်းအရာများဖြစ်သည့် အကြောင်းအရာများဖြစ်သည်။

ဂီဘရူးယားတွင် ကူးစက်မှုကို ကာကွယ်ရေး ဆေးထိုးမှုကို ပြုလုပ်သည့် အစောပိုင်းလေးလတွင် ကျွန်ုပ်တို့သည် မီဒီယာပေါ်တွင် အဆိုပါ ဂီဘရူးယားတွင် ကူးစက်မှုကို ကာကွယ်ရေး ဆေးထိုးမှုကို ပြုလုပ်ခဲ့သည့် အကြောင်းအရာများကို အဆိုပါ ၅၃ ဦး သေဆုံးခဲ့သည်ဟု အဆိုပါ အကြောင်းအရာများကို ဖော်ပြခဲ့သည်။ ဂီဘရူးယားတွင် အဆိုပါ ကူးစက်မှုကို ကာကွယ်ရေး ဆေးထိုးမှုကို ပြုလုပ်ခဲ့သည့် အကြောင်းအရာများကို တွင် အဆိုပါ ကူးစက်မှုကို ကာကွယ်ရေး ဆေးထိုးမှုကို ပြုလုပ်ခဲ့သည့် အကြောင်းအရာများကို နှိုးဆော်ခဲ့သည်။ အဆိုပါ အကြောင်းအရာများသည် အဆိုပါ ကူးစက်မှုကို ကာကွယ်ရေး ဆေးထိုးမှုကို ပြုလုပ်ခဲ့သည့် အကြောင်းအရာများကို တွင် အဆိုပါ အကြောင်းအရာများကို အနည်းငယ်ပြုလုပ်ခဲ့သည်။ ထိုသို့သော အကြောင်းအရာများကို ပြုလုပ်ခြင်းသည် နောက်ဆုံးသော အကြောင်းအရာများကို စိတ်မကောင်းစေပါသည်။

article_summary: Un post en redes sociales afirmó que 53 muertes en Gibraltar ocurrieron por la vacuna contra el COVID-19. Sin embargo, las autoridades sanitarias y organismos internacionales destacaron que esos fallecimientos estaban relacionados con la infección por el virus, no con la vacuna. Se subrayó la importancia de diferenciar correlación y causalidad, ya que las muertes se registraron en un contexto de alta incidencia del virus en la región.

article_content:
A recent social media post claims that PCR tests—the laboratory technique commonly used to detect viral infections such as COVID-19—“come with a positive or negative result and doctors know which one to give to each person.” This assertion implies that the outcomes of PCR tests are predetermined and that medical professionals intentionally assign results regardless of the actual test findings. To evaluate this claim, it is essential to understand how PCR tests work, the role of healthcare providers in interpreting results, and the safeguards in place to ensure accuracy and integrity in medical testing.

Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) testing is a scientific method used to amplify and detect genetic material from pathogens, such as viruses. In the context of infectious disease diagnosis, PCR tests are valued for their sensitivity and specificity. The process typically involves collecting a sample from the patient (commonly a nasal or throat swab), extracting genetic material, and using specific reagents and cycling temperatures to amplify targeted sequences. The outcome—positive or negative—depends entirely on whether the target genetic sequence is present in the sample.

Laboratory technicians, not doctors, are responsible for running PCR tests and interpreting the technical results produced by the testing equipment. These results are generated by automated systems based on established scientific protocols. The data, typically in the form of amplification curves and cycle threshold values, are analyzed to determine whether the target pathogen is present. Laboratory processes are subject to strict regulatory controls and routine quality assurance measures to prevent errors or manipulation.

Once the laboratory completes the test, the result is communicated to the ordering clinician, who then discusses it with the patient and makes recommendations for treatment or isolation if necessary. The assertion that “doctors know which one to give to each person” suggests intentional misrepresentation of test results by medical professionals. In reality, doctors do not control the outcome of PCR assays; they rely on the objective results provided by the laboratory.

Healthcare systems have numerous checks and balances in place to ensure the accuracy of diagnostic testing. Laboratories are required to follow standardized procedures, use validated equipment and reagents, and participate in external quality assessments. Falsifying medical test results is a serious breach of professional ethics and, in most jurisdictions, is illegal. Medical professionals are trained to interpret and communicate test results honestly, and deliberate misrepresentation would jeopardize patient safety and public trust.

It is important to recognize that, like any diagnostic test, PCR assays are not infallible. False positives and false negatives can occur due to factors such as sample contamination, improper collection, or technical limitations. However, such errors are rare when protocols are properly followed, and they do not reflect intentional manipulation by doctors.

In summary, the claim that PCR tests are assigned positive or negative results at the discretion of doctors is unfounded. The results are determined by scientific analysis of biological samples in controlled laboratory environments, and medical professionals play no role in altering or assigning those results. Public confidence in medical testing relies on the integrity of laboratory and clinical practices, which are upheld by rigorous standards and ethical obligations.

In recent weeks, a social media post has gained traction claiming that Israel reported zero deaths from COVID-19 due to the discovery of a "cure" for the virus made from lemon and baking soda. This statement has caused confusion and curiosity among many, prompting questions about its accuracy and the existence of such a remedy.

To understand this claim, it is important to examine the background of COVID-19 in Israel and the scientific validity of using lemon and baking soda as a treatment for the virus. Israel, like many countries, faced significant challenges during the COVID-19 pandemic, including multiple waves of infections, hospitalizations, and deaths. The country implemented strict public health measures, a successful vaccination campaign, and invested heavily in medical infrastructure to combat the spread of the virus.

Official data from the Israeli Ministry of Health and international health organizations show that Israel did experience COVID-19-related deaths throughout the pandemic. The country’s mortality figures were closely monitored, and detailed statistics were made publicly available. At no point did the official records indicate that Israel had zero deaths from the virus, neither before nor after the introduction of vaccines or any purported cures.

The second part of the claim—the existence of a cure made from lemon and baking soda—also warrants scrutiny. Lemon is a common citrus fruit, and baking soda is a household chemical often used for cleaning and baking. Both substances have a long history of home use, sometimes as part of folk remedies for minor ailments like sore throats or indigestion. However, there is no scientific evidence to support the assertion that consuming lemon and baking soda can cure, prevent, or treat COVID-19.

COVID-19 is caused by the SARS-CoV-2 virus, and its treatment requires targeted antiviral therapies, supportive medical care, and, importantly, vaccination to prevent severe outcomes. The World Health Organization, the Israeli Ministry of Health, and medical experts worldwide have consistently warned against relying on unproven home remedies for COVID-19. While maintaining good nutrition and hydration is beneficial for overall health, there is no credible research suggesting that lemon and baking soda possess antiviral properties effective against SARS-CoV-2.

The spread of misinformation regarding miracle cures and home remedies has been a persistent challenge throughout the pandemic. Such claims can be harmful, as they may lead individuals to forgo proven medical treatments or ignore public health guidance. In Israel, the reduction in COVID-19 mortality rates was largely attributed to widespread vaccination, the use of approved antiviral medications, improved testing, and robust healthcare responses—none of which involved lemon and baking soda as a cure.

In conclusion, the claim that Israel had zero COVID-19 deaths because of a lemon and baking soda cure is false. Official records confirm that Israel, like other nations, experienced COVID-19 fatalities and managed its response using evidence-based medical interventions—not unproven home remedies. It is crucial to rely on verified information and scientific consensus when evaluating claims about health and disease prevention.

In recent years, the development and distribution of COVID-19 mRNA vaccines have generated widespread public debate and, at times, misinformation. One claim circulating on social media asserts that the COVID-19 mRNA vaccine is "not a vaccine." To assess the accuracy of this statement, it is important to examine both the definition of vaccines and the scientific principles underlying mRNA vaccine technology.

Vaccines are biological preparations designed to provide immunity against specific infectious diseases. Traditionally, vaccines have been made using weakened or inactivated forms of a virus or bacterium, or by using a piece of the pathogen, such as a protein. These substances stimulate the immune system to recognize and combat the real pathogen if the body is exposed in the future.

The COVID-19 mRNA vaccines, such as those developed by Pfizer-BioNTech and Moderna, use a different but scientifically established approach. Instead of introducing an inactivated virus or a protein directly, they deliver a small piece of genetic material called messenger RNA (mRNA) into the body's cells. This mRNA contains instructions for the cells to produce a harmless fragment of the coronavirus spike protein. The immune system then recognizes this protein as foreign and mounts an immune response, producing antibodies and training immune cells to respond if the person later encounters the actual virus.

The claim that mRNA vaccines "are not vaccines" appears to stem from a misunderstanding of what constitutes a vaccine. The fundamental purpose of a vaccine is to prepare the immune system to fight off a specific infection. mRNA vaccines meet this definition: they train the immune system to recognize the coronavirus without causing disease, thereby reducing the risk of severe illness, hospitalization, and death.

Moreover, the scientific and medical communities classify mRNA vaccines as vaccines because they fulfill the core criteria: they are administered to healthy individuals to induce immunity and prevent disease. The definition of a vaccine does not require the use of live or inactivated pathogens; it encompasses any preparation that stimulates an immune response against a disease-causing agent.

It is important to note that while mRNA vaccines represent a newer technology, they do not fundamentally differ from other vaccines in their purpose or function. The innovation lies in the method of delivery—using mRNA rather than viral proteins or inactivated viruses—but the outcome is the same: the development of protective immunity.

In conclusion, the statement that the COVID-19 mRNA vaccine is "not a vaccine" is inaccurate. Despite differences in technology, mRNA vaccines align with the established scientific definition of a vaccine. They are designed to stimulate the immune system and provide protection against COVID-19. Claims to the contrary are unsupported by scientific evidence and misunderstand vaccine technology and terminology.

A social media post has been circulating claiming that “vaccine mRNA, which creates foreign proteins in our body, modifies our DNA.” This statement raises concerns about the mechanisms of mRNA vaccines and their potential effects on human genetics. This article examines the accuracy of these claims, providing context and a detailed fact-check.

First, it is important to understand how mRNA vaccines, such as those developed for COVID-19, function. mRNA stands for messenger ribonucleic acid, a molecule that carries genetic instructions from DNA in the cell nucleus to the ribosomes, where proteins are made. mRNA vaccines use a synthetically produced version of this molecule, which encodes instructions for cells to produce a specific protein found on the surface of the virus—in the case of COVID-19 vaccines, the spike protein of the SARS-CoV-2 virus.

Once the mRNA is injected, it enters the body’s cells and instructs them to produce the viral spike protein. The immune system recognizes this protein as foreign and mounts a response, creating antibodies and training immune cells to recognize and fight the actual virus if the person is exposed in the future. After this process, the mRNA from the vaccine is broken down and eliminated by normal cellular processes, typically within a few days.

The post correctly states that vaccine mRNA leads to the production of “foreign proteins” in our bodies. However, this is by design and central to how the vaccine stimulates immunity. The spike protein produced is indeed not naturally found in human cells, but its temporary presence is what triggers the immune system to prepare for potential infection.

The core claim that vaccine mRNA “modifies our DNA” is not supported by scientific evidence. Human DNA is contained within the cell nucleus, whereas the mRNA delivered by vaccines remains in the cell’s cytoplasm and does not enter the nucleus. The process by which genetic information is used to make proteins—known as the central dogma of molecular biology—flows from DNA to RNA to protein, not the other way around. There is no mechanism by which the vaccine mRNA can integrate into or alter the DNA of human cells.

Some concerns stem from the fact that certain viruses, such as retroviruses (for example, HIV), can insert their genetic material into human DNA using special enzymes like reverse transcriptase. However, mRNA vaccines do not contain these enzymes, nor do they have the capability to reverse transcribe RNA into DNA or integrate it into the genome.

In summary, while mRNA vaccines do instruct cells to produce a viral protein to prime the immune system, they do not alter or modify human DNA. The body’s natural cellular machinery breaks down and disposes of the mRNA after it has been used, leaving no lasting genetic changes. The claim that mRNA vaccines modify DNA is inaccurate and not supported by current scientific understanding.

ശുചിത്വത്തിന്റെ ആശയം എന്നാൽ, എംആർഎൻഎ വാക്സിനുകൾ കോശങ്ങൾക്ക് വൈറസ് പ്രോട്ടീനുകൾ ഉണ്ടാക്കാൻ നിർദ്ദേശം നൽകി ഇമ്മ്യൂൺ സിസ്റ്റത്തെ തയ്യാറാക്കുന്നു, എന്നാൽ അവ മനുഷ്യ ഡിഎൻഎയെ മാറ്റുന്നില്ല അല്ലെങ്കിൽ അത് മാറ്റുന്നില്ല. കോശ പ്രക്രിയകൾ ഇത് ഉപയോഗിച്ച ശേഷം എംആർഎൻഎ നഷ്ടപ്പെടുത്തി വെളിച്ചത്തിൽ കളയുകയും ചെയ്യുന്നു, ഇത് ഏത് നിലനിൽക്കുന്ന ജീനേറ്റിക് മാറ്റങ്ങളും കാണിക്കുന്നില്ല. എംആർഎൻഎ വാക്സിനുകൾ ഡിഎൻഎ മാറ്റുന്നു എന്ന പ്രസ്താവന അനുസൃതമായി ശരിയല്ല എന്നും പ്രസ്താവന പ്രസ്താവനകൾ പ്രസ്താവനകൾ പ്രകാരമാണ് ഇപ്പോൾ പരിശോധിച്ചിട്ടുള്ളത്.

A recent social media post claims that “France woke up. Doctors, nurses, policemen, firemen are no longer part of the new world order. They renounced to be part of the psychopathic plandemia.” This statement suggests a mass rejection of pandemic policies and alleged global agendas by key public sector professionals in France. The post implies that these professionals have collectively and publicly withdrawn their support for what it calls the “plandemia”—a term often used by conspiracy theorists to describe the COVID-19 pandemic as a planned event.

To fact-check this claim, it is important to examine the context surrounding France’s pandemic response, the actions of healthcare workers and first responders, and the use of language associated with conspiracy theories.

First, the claim that doctors, nurses, police officers, and firefighters in France have “renounced” participation in pandemic measures or a so-called “new world order” is not supported by any credible evidence. Throughout the COVID-19 pandemic, France, like many other countries, implemented public health measures such as mask mandates, social distancing, and vaccination campaigns. These measures were broadly supported and enacted by medical professionals, law enforcement, and emergency services.

While there has been some opposition to specific mandates—such as the requirement for healthcare workers to be vaccinated against COVID-19—this opposition has involved a minority of individuals within those professions. In 2021, for example, some healthcare workers protested mandatory vaccination, and a small number chose to leave their jobs or faced suspension due to non-compliance. However, these instances do not represent a collective renunciation by the majority of professionals.

French police officers and firefighters have also largely followed government guidelines throughout the pandemic. There have been some public demonstrations involving police and emergency personnel, but these were generally related to working conditions or vaccine mandates, not a wholesale rejection of pandemic policies or alignment with conspiracy theories about a “new world order.”

The use of the term “plandemia” is notable. This word is commonly used in online conspiracy theory circles to suggest that the COVID-19 pandemic was orchestrated for nefarious purposes. There is no evidence to support such a theory, and it is widely rejected by the scientific and medical communities worldwide.

In summary, the claim that French doctors, nurses, police officers, and firefighters have collectively rejected pandemic policies or the existence of the pandemic itself is false. While there have been individual protests and disagreements over specific mandates, the vast majority of these professionals have continued to serve the public and follow established guidelines. The assertion that they have renounced their roles in response to a “psychopathic plandemia” is unfounded and reflects misinformation rather than documented fact.

Мануэль Элькин Патаррой — международно известный иммунолог, наиболее известный разработкой первой в мире синтетической вакцины против малярии. В ходе пандемии коронавируса он часто появлялся в СМИ, обсуждая разработку вакцин, иммунологию и стратегии общественного здравоохранения. В заключение, хотя доктор Мануэль Элькин Патаррой постоянно выступал за осторожность, прозрачность и строгую научную оценку всех вакцин от коронавируса, утверждение о том, что он выступил с конкретными предупреждениями относительно вакцины Спутник V, является неточным. Пользователям социальных сетей рекомендуется обращаться за информацией к надежным источникам и учитывать более широкий контекст экспертизных заявлений.

A recent social media post claims that "11 people have been arrested in a Lidl shopping mall while being positive for COVID-19." This claim has generated significant attention and concern online, prompting questions about the circumstances, public safety protocols, and the accuracy of the information. In this fact-check, we examine the claim’s validity, provide background on COVID-19 protocols in public spaces, and analyze available evidence to clarify what actually happened.

Firstly, it is important to note that Lidl is a prominent international supermarket chain with locations across Europe and beyond. Shopping centers and grocery stores like Lidl have been the focus of heightened health and safety measures since the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic. Many countries have implemented strict regulations regarding mask-wearing, social distancing, and, during certain periods, entry restrictions for those diagnosed with COVID-19.

The core claim of the social media post is that 11 people, reportedly COVID-19 positive, were arrested inside a Lidl shopping mall. To assess this, we must consider several aspects: the plausibility of mass arrests for COVID-19 status, how authorities handle known COVID-19 cases in public, and whether any official reports or news articles corroborate such an incident.

In most countries, individuals who have tested positive for COVID-19 are legally required to self-isolate and avoid public spaces to prevent the spread of the virus. Breaking isolation rules can result in fines or, in some cases, legal action. However, mass arrests for COVID-19 violations in retail settings are extremely rare. Law enforcement typically relies on health authorities to track and enforce isolation orders, and arrests are generally reserved for repeated or egregious violations.

A search of recent news reports and official statements reveals no credible evidence supporting the claim that 11 people were arrested in a Lidl location for being COVID-19 positive. Such an incident would likely attract widespread media coverage, given its unusual nature and public health implications. Instead, available information suggests that while isolated incidents of individuals breaching isolation have occurred in various regions, these are typically handled on a case-by-case basis and rarely involve multiple simultaneous arrests in a single location.

It is also important to consider the challenges in identifying COVID-19 positive individuals in public without prior knowledge or notification. Unless someone is visibly symptomatic and admits to having tested positive, it would be difficult for store staff or authorities to confirm their health status on the spot.

In summary, there is no substantive evidence to support the claim that 11 individuals were arrested in a Lidl shopping mall while being positive for COVID-19. The claim appears to be unsubstantiated and lacks confirmation from any official or reputable news sources. As always, it is important for the public to verify information, especially regarding health and safety issues, before sharing or acting upon such claims.

पहले यह ध्यान रखना महत्वपूर्ण है कि लिडल एक प्रमुख अंतरराष्ट्रीय सुपरमार्केट शॉपिंग चेन है जो यूरोप और उसके बाहर विभिन्न स्थानों पर स्थित है। कोरोना वायरस महामारी के आरंभ के बाद से शॉपिंग सेंटर और ग्राहक सुविधाओं जैसे लिडल के ऐसे स्थान जनसामान्य स्वास्थ्य और सुरक्षा के नियमों के तहत ध्यान के केंद्र में रहे हैं। कई देशों ने मास्क पहनने, सामाजिक दूरी बनाए रखने और कुछ अवधि के दौरान कोरोना वायरस संक्रमित व्यक्तियों के प्रवेश पर प्रतिबंध लगाने के लिए गंभीर नियमों को लागू किया है।

सोशल मीडिया पोस्ट का नामकरण यह है कि लिडल शॉपिंग मैल में 11 व्यक्ति, जो कोरोना वायरस संक्रमित बताए जा रहे हैं, गिरफ्तार किए गए। इस बारे में जांच करने के लिए हम कई पहलुओं को ध्यान में रखेंगे: कोरोना वायरस के अवस्था के लिए महामारी के बारे में बड़े पैमाने पर गिरफ्तारी की संभावना, सार्वजनिक स्थानों में ज्ञात कोरोना वायरस मामलों के बारे में अधिकारियों के कैसे व्यवहार करते हैं, और क्या कोई आधिकारिक रिपोर्ट या समाचार ऐसे घटना की पुष्टि करते हैं।

अधिकांश देशों में, कोरोना वायरस के पॉजिटिव व्यक्ति को कानूनी रूप से स्व-निर्वाह करना आवश्यक है और जनसामान्य स्थानों से दूर रहना आवश्यक है ताकि वायरस के फैलाव को रोका जा सके। इस नियम के उल्लंघन करने के लिए जुर्माना या कुछ मामलों में कानूनी कार्यवाही हो सकती है। हालांकि, रेटेल स्थानों में कोरोना वायरस उल्लंघन के लिए महामारी के बारे में बड़े पैमाने पर गिरफ्तारी बहुत दुर्लभ है। पुलिस आमतौर पर स्वास्थ्य अधिकारियों पर निर्भर करती है जो विभिन्न नियमों के लिए ट्रैक करते हैं और इसे लागू करते हैं, और गिरफ्तारी आमतौर पर बार-बार या भारी उल्लंघन के मामले में ही होती है।

हाल के समाचार रिपोर्ट और आधिकारिक कथनों के खोज के दौरान, लिडल के किसी स्थान पर कोरोना वायरस के पॉजिटिव होने के बावजूद 11 व्यक्तियों के गिरफ्तार करने के बारे में कोई विश्वसनीय साक्ष्य नहीं मिला है। ऐसी घटना के कारण अप्रत्यक्ष रूप से जनसामान्य ध्यान की आकर्षित करेगी, इसके अलावा जन स्वास्थ्य के अस्तित्व के संबंध में असामान्य प्रकृति के कारण। बजाए इसके, उपलब्ध जानकारी इस बात को सुझाव देती है कि जबकि कई क्षेत्रों में व्यक्तियों के निर्वाह के उल्लंघन के व्यक्तिगत मामले हो सकते हैं, लेकिन इनके बारे में कम बार एक स्थान में एक साथ बहुत सारे गिरफ्तारी आमतौर पर नहीं होती है।

इसके अलावा, यह ध्यान रखना महत्वपूर्ण है कि बिना पहले ज्ञान या सूचना के जनसामान्य स्थानों में कोरोना वायरस के पॉजिटिव व्यक्ति की पहचान करना कठिन हो सकता है। अगर कोई व्यक्ति निश्चित लक्षण दिखाता है और अपने कोरोना वायरस के पॉजिटिव रहे होने के बारे में स्वीकृति देता है, तो अन्यथा स्टोर कर्मचारी या अधिकारियों द्वारा तत्काल उनकी स्वास्थ्य स्थिति की पुष्टि करना कठिन हो सकता है।

सारांश के रूप में, कोरोना वायरस के पॉजिटिव होने के बावजूद लिडल शॉपिंग मैल में 11 व्यक्तियों के गिरफ्तार करने के बारे में कोई विश्वसनीय साक्ष्य नहीं है। इस कथन की वैधता नहीं है और इसकी पुष्टि कोई आधिकारिक या विश्वसनीय समाचार स्रोत द्वारा नहीं की गई है। हमेशा जनता को विशेष रूप से स्वास्थ्य और सुरक्षा के मुद्दों के बारे में जानकारी के बारे में पहले जांच करना महत्वपूर्ण है, जिसके बाद ऐसे कथनों को साझा करने या उन पर कार्य करने के लिए तैयार हो सकते हैं।

In recent days, a social media post has circulated claiming that “cases of children with COVID-19 in Madrid hospitals emergency rooms soar.” This alarming statement has generated concern among parents and the wider community, raising questions about the current epidemiological situation in Madrid and the potential impact on pediatric healthcare facilities.

To assess the validity of this claim, it is essential to examine the available data and context surrounding COVID-19 cases among children in Madrid, as well as to consider the broader trends in pediatric emergency room visits.

**Background and Context**

Since the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic, children have generally experienced milder symptoms compared to adults, and hospitalization rates among pediatric populations have remained relatively low. However, there have been periods during which surges in COVID-19 cases have led to increased numbers of children seeking medical attention, particularly during waves dominated by highly transmissible variants.

In Madrid, as in other parts of Spain and Europe, public health authorities have closely monitored infection rates, hospital admissions, and emergency room activity. Seasonal trends also play a role: during the autumn and winter months, pediatric emergency rooms typically see an uptick in visits due to respiratory illnesses like influenza and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), which can overlap with COVID-19 symptoms and complicate diagnosis.

**Fact-Checking the Core Claim**

The claim that cases of children with COVID-19 in Madrid’s hospital emergency rooms are “soaring” suggests a sudden and significant increase in pediatric COVID-19 cases severe enough to require urgent medical care.

Official health bulletins from Madrid’s regional health authorities indicate that, while there can be periodic increases in COVID-19 cases among children—often corresponding with broader waves of community transmission—there is currently no evidence of an extraordinary or unprecedented surge at the time of this article.

Pediatric emergency departments in Madrid have reported increases in overall visits, particularly during periods of high viral circulation. However, much of this increase is attributed to a combination of seasonal viruses, not exclusively COVID-19. Health professionals note that, while some children do present with COVID-19 symptoms, most cases are mild and do not require hospitalization. The proportion of children testing positive for COVID-19 among all pediatric emergency cases has remained relatively stable in recent months, with no sharp spike that would justify the term “soaring.”

It is also important to consider the possibility of heightened parental concern leading to increased emergency room visits for mild symptoms, even when COVID-19 is not confirmed.

**Conclusion**

While there have been periods of increased pediatric emergency room activity in Madrid, particularly during respiratory virus season, there is currently no substantiated evidence to support the claim that cases of children with COVID-19 in Madrid hospital emergency rooms are soaring. The overall number of pediatric COVID-19 emergencies remains within expected seasonal fluctuations, and most cases are mild. The claim appears to exaggerate the current situation and does not align with the most recent data from healthcare authorities and hospitals in Madrid. Parents are advised to remain vigilant but not alarmed, and to consult healthcare professionals for guidance on when emergency care is necessary.

Ši įspūdinga deklaracija sukėlė susirūpinimą tėvų ir plačiau susijusios bendruomenės dėl, kyla klausimų apie dabartinę epideminią situaciją Madrido ir potencialų poveikį pediatriniams sveikatos priežiūros įstaigoms.

Norint įvertinti šios deklaracijos teisumą, svarbu apsvarstyti prieinamą duomenų ir kontekstą, susijusį su vaikų su COVID-19 atvejais Madrido, taip pat apsvarstyti plačiąją pediatrinių ambulantiškųjų klinikų vizitų tendencijas.

**Kontekstas ir pagrindinė informacija**

Nuo pandemijos pradžios vaikai dažniau patiria mažiau sunkių simptomų nei suaugusieji, o hospitalizavimo procentas vaikų populiacijoje iki šiol išlieka mažai. Tačiau buvo periodai, kai COVID-19 atvejų surišimas padidino vaikų, siekiančių medicininių paslaugų skaičių, ypač tada, kai dominavę labai perduodamos variantų bangos.

Madride, kaip ir kitose Šiaurės Europos šalyse, sveikatos apsaugos institucijos stovėjo prieš kovos su infekcijų skirstymu, ligoninėmis įtraukimais ir ambulantiškųjų klinikų veikla. Sezoninės tendencijos taip pat turi svarbų įtaką: žiemą ir rudens mėnesius pediatrinių ambulantiškųjų klinikų vizitai dažnai kyla dėl kvėpimo takų ligų, tokios kaip influenzos ir kvėpimo takų atsiradimo virusas (RSV), kurios gali susikirti su COVID-19 simptomais ir sudėtinginti diagnozę.

**Tiesioginės patikros pagrindinis teiginys**

Teiginys, kad „vaikų su COVID-19 atvejai Madrido klinikų ambulantiškose klinikose didėja“, reiškia šokį ir reikšmingą padidėjimą pediatrinių COVID-19 atvejų skaičiui, pakankamai sunkiems, kad būtų reikalinga akimirksnio medicininė pagalba.

Oficialūs sveikatos informacijos dokumentai, pateikti Madrido regioninės sveikatos apsaugos institucijų, rodo, kad nors gali būti periodiškai padidėjusios vaikų su COVID-19 atvejai – dažnai atitinka plėtojamos bendruomenės perleidimo bangas – šiuo straipsnio publikavimo metu nėra įrodymų apie nereikšmingą ar net nepavyzdėtą šokį.

Madrido pediatrinių ambulantiškųjų klinikų ataskaitose nurodyta, kad bendras vizitų skaičius padidėja, ypač tada, kai viruso skirstymas yra didelis. Tačiau daugelis šio padidėjimo yra susiję su sezoniniais virusais, o ne tik su COVID-19. Sveikatos darbuotojai pastebi, kad nors kai kurie vaikai turi COVID-19 simptomų, daugelis atvejų yra lengvai gydomi ir nereikalauja ligoninės įtraukimo. Vaikų, teigiantis teigiamai COVID-19, procentas visų pediatrinių ambulantiškųjų klinikų atvejų nesikeičia per pastaruosius mėnesius, be didelio šoko, kuris būtų patvirtintas „didėjimo“ terminu.

Taip pat svarbu įvertinti galimybę, kad didesnis tėvų susirūpinimas gali sukelti ambulantiškųjų klinikų vizitus dėl lengvų simptomų, net kai neigiamai patvirtinta COVID-19.

**Išvados**

A recent social media post has been circulating the claim that guava leaf may cure or prevent COVID-19. The statement has gained traction, with some users sharing home remedies involving guava leaf tea or extracts as a potential safeguard against the coronavirus. With ongoing concerns about COVID-19 and a persistent appetite for natural remedies, it is important to assess the accuracy of this claim.

Guava leaves have traditionally been used in various cultures for their purported medicinal properties. They are commonly employed in folk medicine for digestive issues, inflammation, and as a remedy for certain infections. The leaves are known to contain a range of bioactive compounds, including antioxidants and antimicrobial agents, which have led to their use in teas and herbal preparations.

Since the emergence of the COVID-19 pandemic, many natural remedies have been proposed as possible treatments or preventatives. COVID-19 is caused by the SARS-CoV-2 virus and can lead to severe respiratory illness. Scientific research has focused primarily on vaccines, antiviral medications, and public health measures as the main tools to combat the spread of the virus and reduce the severity of illness.

To date, there is no scientific evidence that guava leaf can cure or prevent COVID-19. No peer-reviewed clinical trials or studies have demonstrated that guava leaf extracts, teas, or supplements have any direct effect on the SARS-CoV-2 virus or on the course of COVID-19 in humans. While guava leaves may contain compounds with general antimicrobial or anti-inflammatory properties, these characteristics have not been shown to specifically target or neutralize the coronavirus.

The World Health Organization and leading health authorities consistently warn against relying on unproven natural remedies as substitutes for evidence-based treatments and preventative measures. Vaccination, wearing masks, maintaining social distance, and hand hygiene remain the most effective strategies for preventing COVID-19. Experimental treatments and home remedies, such as those involving guava leaves, should not replace medical advice or scientifically validated interventions.

It is understandable that individuals seek alternative ways to protect themselves and their families during a global health crisis. However, spreading misinformation about the ability of guava leaf to cure or prevent COVID-19 can be dangerous. People who believe in such claims may delay seeking appropriate medical care or forego proven methods of protection, increasing their risk of severe illness.

In conclusion, the claim that guava leaf may cure or prevent COVID-19 is not supported by scientific evidence. While guava leaves may have certain health benefits, they should not be considered a treatment or preventative measure for COVID-19. It is crucial to rely on trusted medical sources and adhere to guidelines from public health authorities to protect against the virus.

A claim circulating on social media asserts that PCR tests, commonly used to detect COVID-19, do not actually identify SARS-CoV-2—the virus responsible for COVID-19—but instead detect "endogenous gene sequences" from the patient. This claim raises questions about the validity of COVID-19 testing and has contributed to misinformation during the pandemic. A detailed examination of the science behind PCR tests and their application in COVID-19 diagnosis reveals that this claim is unfounded.

Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) is a well-established laboratory technique developed in the 1980s. It is designed to amplify and detect specific genetic material, making it possible to identify even tiny amounts of DNA or RNA from a given organism. In the context of COVID-19, the most widely used method is reverse transcription PCR (RT-PCR), which detects the presence of SARS-CoV-2 RNA in patient samples, most often taken from the nose or throat.

The core of the claim is that PCR tests supposedly detect genetic material that is naturally present in humans, not the virus. In reality, when designing PCR tests for COVID-19, scientists select unique sequences of the virus's RNA that are not found in human DNA or RNA. These unique sequences act as genetic fingerprints for SARS-CoV-2. The test uses small pieces of synthetic genetic material called primers, which bind specifically to the viral RNA if it is present in the sample. If the viral RNA is absent, the primers do not bind, and the test returns a negative result.

To ensure accuracy, before being approved for widespread use, PCR tests undergo rigorous validation. Regulators and scientists verify that the primers and probes do not cross-react with human genes or with genetic material from other viruses and bacteria that might be present in respiratory samples. This process helps prevent false positives that could result from detecting non-viral, endogenous genetic material.

It is true that PCR is a highly sensitive method, and contamination or technical errors can sometimes lead to inaccurate results. However, the overwhelming evidence from laboratory studies and real-world testing supports the conclusion that, when properly performed, PCR tests specifically detect SARS-CoV-2 and do not mistakenly identify human genetic material as the virus.

The misconception that PCR tests detect "endogenous gene sequences" may stem from misunderstandings about how the technology works or from misinterpretations of technical details. While every person naturally carries their own DNA and RNA, the regions targeted by SARS-CoV-2 PCR tests are carefully selected to exclude any overlap with the human genome.

In summary, the claim that PCR tests for COVID-19 detect only endogenous gene sequences rather than SARS-CoV-2 is false. PCR testing remains one of the most reliable and specific tools for identifying active COVID-19 infections, thanks to its precise targeting of unique viral genetic sequences. Public confidence in this technology is justified by its scientific foundation and careful validation procedures.

दावे के केंद्र यह है कि पीसीआर टेस्ट केवल मनुष्य में प्राकृतिक रूप से उपस्थित आनुवांशिक सामग्री को पहचानते हैं, न कि वायरस। वास्तविकता में, कोरोनावायरस के लिए पीसीआर टेस्ट डिज़ाइन करते समय वैज्ञानिक वायरस के आरएनए के विशिष्ट अनुक्रम का चयन करते हैं जो मनुष्य के डीएनए या आरएनए में नहीं मिलते हैं। इन विशिष्ट अनुक्रमों का आनुवांशिक प्रिंट के रूप में कार्य करते हैं। टेस्ट छोटे टुकड़ों के संश्लेषित आनुवांशिक सामग्री के रूप में प्रयोग किए जाने वाले प्रारंभकों का उपयोग करते हैं, जो यदि नमूना में वायरस उपस्थित हो तो विशेष रूप से वायरल आरएनए के साथ बंधते हैं। यदि वायरल आरएनए नहीं होता है, तो प्रारंभक बंध नहीं लगाते हैं और टेस्ट नकारात्मक परिणाम देता है।

सटीकता के लिए, पीसीआर टेस्ट के व्यापक उपयोग के लिए अनुमोदन से पहले इन टेस्ट को गृहीत करने योग्यता के लिए गंभीर निरीक्षण के अंतर्गत ले लिया जाता है। नियामक और वैज्ञानिक निरीक्षण करते हैं कि प्रारंभक और प्रोब्स मनुष्य के जीन या श्वास नली नमूनों में मौजूद अन्य वायरस और बैक्टीरिया के आनुवांशिक सामग्री से प्रतिक्रिया नहीं करते हैं। इस प्रक्रिया गलत सकारात्मक परिणाम को रोकती है जो अ-वायरल, अंतर्निहित आनुवांशिक सामग्री के पता लगाने के कारण हो सकते हैं।

यह सच है कि पीसीआर एक बहुत संवेदनशील विधि है, और संदूषण या तकनीकी त्रुटियों के कारण अक्सर असटीक परिणाम हो सकते हैं। हालांकि, प्रयोगशाला अध्ययनों और वास्तविक दुनिया के टेस्टिंग के आधार पर अत्यधिक प्रमाण इस निष्कर्ष के विरोध में है कि, जब ठीक से किया जाए तो पीसीआर टेस्ट सार्स-कोव-2 के विशिष्ट रूप से पहचानते हैं और मनुष्य के आनुवांशिक सामग्री को गलत रूप से वायरस के रूप में पहचानने के बजाय नहीं।

पीसीआर टेस्ट के अंतर्निहित जीन अनुक्रम के अनुसार दावा के भ्रम के कारण तकनीक के काम के बारे में गलत समझ या तकनीकी विवरण के गलत व्याख्या हो सकती है। हर व्यक्ति में अपना डीएनए और आरएनए प्राकृतिक रूप से उपस्थित होता है, लेकिन सार्स-कोव-2 पीसीआर टेस्ट के लक्ष्य विशेष रूप से तैयार किए गए अनुक्रम विशिष्ट रूप से मनुष्य जीनोम के क्षेत्रों के ओवरलैप को बाहर रखते हैं।

संक्षेप में, कोरोनावायरस के पीसीआर टेस्ट केवल अंतर्निहित जीन अनुक्रम को पहचानते हैं न कि सार्स-कोव-2 के बारे में दावा गलत है। पीसीआर टेस्टिंग कोरोनावायरस निदान के लिए सबसे विश्वसनीय और विशिष्ट उपकरणों में से एक रहता है, क्योंकि इसके विशिष्ट वायरल आनुवांशिक अनुक्रम के लक्ष्य के लिए धन्यवाद। इस तकनीक के सामान्य विश्वास के आधार पर इसके वैज्ञानिक आधार और ध्यानपूर्वक निरीक्षण प्रक्रियाओं के आधार पर यह वैध है।

A widely circulated WhatsApp message is urging users to "Fill in this form to consult your covid-19 vaccination site." The message provides a link and instructs recipients to enter personal details to purportedly receive information about where they can obtain a COVID-19 vaccine. Given the sensitivity of health information and the prevalence of scams during the pandemic, this claim warrants careful scrutiny.

Context and Background

Since the start of COVID-19 vaccination campaigns, health authorities around the world have implemented a variety of methods to inform citizens about vaccine availability and locations. Official government websites, verified mobile apps, and public health phone lines have been the most commonly promoted channels. These platforms require secure handling of personal data and often ask for minimal information, such as age group and location, to direct individuals to appropriate vaccination sites.

WhatsApp, a popular messaging platform, has been both a tool for rapid dissemination of legitimate information and a vector for misinformation. The informal nature of WhatsApp communications, combined with the ease of forwarding messages, has made it difficult for users to distinguish between official announcements and fraudulent schemes. During the pandemic, several scams have surfaced, including fake vaccination appointment links, phishing attempts, and misinformation about vaccine safety.

Fact-Checking Analysis

Upon analysis, the WhatsApp message in question raises several red flags. Firstly, health authorities typically do not use third-party forms circulated via social media to collect personal information for vaccination site consultations. Instead, they rely on official channels, such as government health websites or verified health apps, which ensure data protection and privacy.

Secondly, the message lacks specific details, such as the name of the health authority, a verifiable source, or any direct link to government services. Legitimate communications from health organizations generally include clear branding, contact information, and direct links to official portals. The generic request to "fill in this form" without any additional context is commonly associated with phishing attempts designed to harvest personal information.

Thirdly, experts warn against clicking on unsolicited links or providing sensitive details through unknown forms. Scammers often exploit public concern during health crises to gain access to personal data, which can be used for identity theft or other malicious activities. If a user receives such a WhatsApp message, the recommended action is to visit the official website of their country's health department or consult trusted sources for vaccination information.

Conclusion

The claim that filling out a form received via WhatsApp is a safe or official method to consult a COVID-19 vaccination site is misleading and potentially unsafe. There is no evidence that health authorities are distributing such forms through informal messaging platforms. Individuals seeking vaccination site information should use official government channels and avoid sharing personal information through unverified forms distributed via WhatsApp. Staying alert to the source and authenticity of health-related messages remains crucial as misinformation and scams continue to circulate online.

Pesan yang beredar luas di WhatsApp mengajak pengguna untuk "Isi formulir ini untuk konsultasi lokasi vaksinasi covid-19 Anda." Mengingat sensitivitas informasi kesehatan dan maraknya penipuan selama pandemi, klaim ini perlu diperiksa secara cermat.

Latar Belakang dan Konteks

Sejak awal kampanye vaksinasi covid-19, otoritas kesehatan di berbagai negara telah menerapkan berbagai metode untuk memberi informasi kepada masyarakat mengenai ketersediaan vaksin dan lokasinya. Situs resmi pemerintah, aplikasi seluler yang terverifikasi, dan layanan telepon kesehatan publik adalah saluran yang paling sering dipromosikan. Platform-platform ini memerlukan penanganan data pribadi yang aman dan biasanya hanya meminta informasi minimal, seperti kelompok usia dan lokasi, untuk mengarahkan individu ke tempat vaksinasi yang sesuai.

WhatsApp, platform pesan yang populer, berfungsi sebagai alat untuk menyebarkan informasi resmi secara cepat sekaligus menjadi media penyebaran informasi yang tidak benar. Sifat informal komunikasi di WhatsApp, ditambah kemudahan meneruskan pesan, membuat pengguna sulit membedakan antara pengumuman resmi dan skema penipuan. Selama pandemi, berbagai skema penipuan muncul, termasuk tautan palsu untuk janji vaksinasi, upaya phishing, dan informasi palsu mengenai keamanan vaksin.

Analisis Pemeriksaan Fakta

Setelah dianalisis, pesan WhatsApp yang ditanyakan menunjukkan beberapa tanda meragukan. Pertama, otoritas kesehatan biasanya tidak menggunakan formulir pihak ketiga yang beredar melalui media sosial untuk mengumpulkan informasi pribadi guna konsultasi lokasi vaksinasi. Sebaliknya, mereka mengandalkan saluran resmi, seperti situs kesehatan pemerintah atau aplikasi kesehatan yang terverifikasi, yang memastikan perlindungan dan privasi data.

Kedua, pesan tersebut tidak menyertakan detail spesifik, seperti nama otoritas kesehatan, sumber yang dapat diverifikasi, atau tautan langsung ke layanan pemerintah. Komunikasi resmi dari organisasi kesehatan biasanya mencakup merek yang jelas, informasi kontak, dan tautan langsung ke portal resmi. Permintaan umum untuk "isi formulir ini" tanpa konteks tambahan sering dikaitkan dengan upaya phishing yang bertujuan mengumpulkan informasi pribadi.

Ketiga, para ahli memperingatkan agar tidak mengklik tautan yang tidak diharapkan atau memberikan informasi sensitif melalui formulir yang tidak dikenal. Penipu sering memanfaatkan kekhawatiran publik selama krisis kesehatan untuk mengakses data pribadi, yang dapat digunakan untuk pencurian identitas atau aktivitas jahat lainnya. Jika seseorang menerima pesan WhatsApp seperti ini, langkah yang direkomendasikan adalah mengunjungi situs resmi departemen kesehatan negara mereka atau konsultasi sumber yang dapat dipercaya untuk informasi vaksinasi.

Kesimpulan

Klaim bahwa mengisi formulir yang diterima melalui WhatsApp merupakan metode aman atau resmi untuk konsultasi lokasi vaksinasi covid-19 adalah salah dan berpotensi berbahaya. Tidak ada bukti bahwa otoritas kesehatan mendistribusikan formulir seperti ini melalui platform pesan informal. Individu yang mencari informasi tentang lokasi vaksinasi sebaiknya menggunakan saluran resmi pemerintah dan menghindari berbagi informasi pribadi melalui formulir yang tidak diverifikasi yang beredar melalui WhatsApp. Tetap waspada terhadap sumber dan keaslian pesan kesehatan tetap penting, karena informasi palsu dan skema penipuan terus beredar di internet.
